title: Felix and the Glasshouse
premise: Mara Iversen, a bridge inspector who measures everything and feels nothing out loud, learns that the glasshouse where they grew up — their grandmother's ruined conservatory, sold decades ago after a family rupture no one will name — is going up for auction. Returning to the town they fled at nineteen, Mara must confront the estranged brother who kept the secrets, the auctioneer's daughter who remembers a different childhood, and the truth about why the glasshouse was really lost. As the bidding date closes in, Mara discovers the house can only be saved by exposing the lie that has held their family together, forcing a choice between belonging and truth. In the end, Mara lets the glasshouse go — but says goodbye properly, out loud, for the first time, and walks away carrying something better than ownership.
about_author: Wren Villalobos is a former structural drafter who spent six years inspecting bridges across the Pacific Northwest before turning to fiction full-time. Their stories examine how people maintain the load-bearing lies of family, and they write from a converted greenhouse on Vashon Island.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. On the Harrow Bridge, Mara measures millimeters of movement and deflects a coworker's friendly question with the practiced smile that ends conversations. A letter arrives: the Alder Street property, including the glasshouse, is entering probate auction. The beat is quiet dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: The Letter with Two Return Addresses
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The letter was forwarded by their brother Dev, whom Mara hasn't spoken to in eleven years. Flashback fragments of the glasshouse: fig trees under fogged panes, grandmother Ruth's hands. Mara drafts three replies and burns none of them. Emotional beat: longing sharpened into resentment.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At work, Mara flags a hairline fracture in a girder that superiors want to ignore; the inspection becomes a mirror for what Mara refuses to inspect in themselves. They request two weeks' leave. Beat: the first small act of honesty, aimed at concrete instead of people.

chapters.title: Alder Street
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, arriving in Corvane. The town is smaller than memory; the glasshouse stands behind chain-link, its panes clouded like cataracts. Dev is already there, measuring the lot for a developer's flyer. Their reunion is all logistics and no language. Beat: two survivors speaking in invoices.

chapters.title: What Dev Kept
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He reveals he's been paying the back taxes quietly for years to keep the auction from happening sooner — and hiding it because Ruth's will named conditions neither sibling has ever met. Beat: loyalty revealed as a burden carried alone, and Mara's guilt arriving late.

chapters.title: The Auctioneer's Daughter
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. June Calloway, running her father's auction house now, recognizes Mara from childhood summers. She offers a private walkthrough and mentions, casually, that her father keeps an inventory file on the estate — including papers Ruth left in the potting shed. Beat: warmth that feels like exposure.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: June's POV. June catalogues the glasshouse contents and finds a sealed envelope labeled 'For whichever child comes back.' Her father instructs her to set it aside; estates are business. But she pockets a photograph instead — young Mara and Dev under the fig tree. Beat: complicity beginning gently.

chapters.title: The Will's Conditions
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Dev finally produces Ruth's will: the estate passes free of auction only if both siblings appear together and read aloud a statement she wrote — a confession of the family rupture. Dev has never told Mara what the statement says. Beat: the past presented as terms and conditions.

chapters.title: Fig Trees Don't Forgive
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The siblings attempt the reading in the empty glasshouse and fail within a paragraph; old accusations surface — who stayed, who left, who let the bank take it. Mara walks out. Beat: proof that proximity without honesty is just weather in a broken structure.

chapters.title: Bridges at Night
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Unable to sleep, Mara inspects the county bridge alone at 3 a.m., talking to the steel the way they can't talk to Dev. A memory surfaces fully for the first time: the night of the rupture, and their father's voice through the glasshouse door. Beat: the buried scene cracking open.

chapters.title: The Night Through Glass
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Mara's POV, age nineteen. The father's debts, the fight, Ruth's stroke that same week, and the moment Mara chose to leave rather than testify to what they saw — leaving Dev to hold the story alone. Beat: understanding, not absolution; Mara sees their own silence as the original betrayal.

chapters.title: June's File
chapters.summary: June's POV. June gives Mara the envelope from the potting shed against her father's wishes. Inside: Ruth's unsent letters, revealing the father's debts were covered by Ruth's own quiet sacrifice — and that she blamed herself, not the children. Beat: the ground shifting under every grudge.

chapters.title: Two Weeks Left
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. With the auction ten days out, Mara tries to interest preservation societies in the glasshouse; all decline — sentiment isn't collateral. Dev, meanwhile, has a developer's offer that would settle his debts. Beat: hope learning the market price of memory.

chapters.title: The Developer's Dinner
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. At the developer's dinner, Dev realizes the offer requires him to sign an affidavit repeating the official version of how the estate was lost — the lie. His whole life he protected the lie to protect Mara; now it costs him the last thing he has. Beat: loyalty reaching its breaking strain.

chapters.title: What the Smile Is For
chapters.summary: June's POV. June confronts her father about the withheld papers; he argues he was protecting everyone, and she hears in him the same logic Dev used. She decides to testify to the envelope's existence if the siblings challenge the sale. Beat: a bystander choosing a side.

chapters.title: Ruth's Statement
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara finally reads Ruth's statement alone: it is not a confession of the children's sins but Ruth's own — and it ends asking them to say, out loud, whatever they each buried. Mara practices saying it in the empty glasshouse and cannot finish. Beat: terror of the plain sentence.

chapters.title: The Fracture
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Back home briefly, Mara files the girder report over superiors' objections and is suspended pending review. Freed of the job's armor, Mara drives back to Corvane overnight. Beat: losing the thing that made avoidance possible.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The auction begins; the developer bids steadily. Before the hammer falls, Mara stands and reads Ruth's statement aloud in front of the whole room — the rupture, the debt, the lie — and Dev joins them mid-page. June confirms the withheld papers. Beat: climax; truth spoken publicly, price be damned.

chapters.title: Hammer Fall
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The sale proceeds anyway — truth doesn't stop markets — and the glasshouse goes to the developer. Dev signs nothing. The siblings stand in the parking lot, hollowed and lighter. Beat: the cost paid in full, and the discovery that it bought something money couldn't.

chapters.title: Salvage Rights
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The developer, embarrassed by publicity, permits one day to salvage what they want. The siblings work the glasshouse together — cuttings from the fig tree, Ruth's tools, the photograph June returns. Beat: grief performed as labor, and labor becoming reconciliation.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. On the last evening, Mara and Dev sit in the stripped glasshouse as the light goes amber through empty panes, and each says the sentence they've owed since they were nineteen — Mara's silence, Dev's protection — plainly, to each other. Beat: the goodbye done properly at last.

chapters.title: New Growth
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, eighteen months later. Mara's suspension resolved into a safety-advocacy role; the fig cutting thrives in Wren-like sunlight on a windowsill. Dev visits monthly. The final image: Mara smiling at a stranger's question — and this time answering it. Beat: belonging rebuilt on truth, portable, unowned.
